newsitem.title: USA: EEI says US power deregulation making big strides.
newsitem.headline: EEI says US power deregulation making big strides.

text.p: U.S. investor-owned utilities are moving quickly toward a deregulated power market, but the change is raising concerns over whether the grid can handle the load, the head of the Edison Electric Institute (EEI) said Wednesday.

"We are substantially ahead of where we were less than a year ago...and much farther along toward competition at all levels than many people are aware," EEI president Thomas Kuhn told a meeting of the New York Society of Security Analysts.
The EEI is a Washington-based trade group representing investor-owned utilities. Its members produce about 75 percent of the country's electricity.
Kuhn said there are currently 284 power marketers licensed with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC), up 71 percent from last year's tally of 166.
With this increase, electricity sales through marketers totalled 134 million megawatt hours through the 1996 third quarter, up 460 percent from a year earlier.
A year ago, California forged the path toward deregulation by enacting laws to restructure the industry, Kuhn said.

New Hampshire, Pennsylvania and Rhode Island have since brought to law similar restructuring plans, while Arizona, Massachusetts, New York and Vermont have adopted plans that are awaiting legislative approval.
All remaining states, with the exception of Tennessee, have addressed restructuring in some way, he said.
"Approximately 30 percent of the U.S. population lives in states that have enacted legislation or adopted final rules for retail competition," Kuhn said.

With widespread outages last summer in the West and bottlenecks threatening parts of the Northeast, high-voltage transmission capacity rather than generating capacity is emerging as the industry's main concern.

"To ensure that our transmission system remains equal to the test, our CEOs have formed a Steering Committee on Reliability. It is working with the DOE (Dept of Energy) Task Force chaired by former Congressman Philip Sharp, with FERC and NERC (North American Electric Reliability Council)," Kuhn said.
New policies and technologies will be addressed to provide electricity to customers in a more efficient manner, he said.
"People must be motivated to add capacity, put in linkages between corridors and develop new technology. Our system must be continually upgraded to accommodate the growing traffic and transactions."
